note: Shimon HaTzaddik, a priest, said he had never eaten the guilt-offering of a nazirite who had become impure, except once. A handsome young man from the South came to him with beautiful eyes and curled locks. Shimon asked why he would destroy such hair. The man said that while shepherding for his father he saw his reflection in a spring, his evil inclination rose up against him, and he swore to shave his hair for the sake of Heaven. Shimon rose, kissed him on the head, and said: may there be more nazirites like you in Israel.
why: The Gemara asked why Rabbi Shimon does not learn from the words "to the Lord" that one can vow to be a nazirite like Samson. The answer: those words are needed to teach that a nazirite vow should be made purely for the sake of Heaven, as this young man's was.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A priest who tells of the one impure nazirite whose offering he ate.

people.name: the man from the South
people.about: A young shepherd who became a nazirite to subdue his pride in his looks.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
An offering a nazirite must bring after becoming ritually impure, after which he starts his term again. Shimon avoided eating it because such nazirites often regretted their vows.
In rabbinic thought, the inner urge that pushes a person toward sin or arrogance.

note: Queen Helene vowed that if her son came home safely from war she would be a nazirite for seven years. He returned and she kept the vow. Then she went up to the Land of Israel, where Beit Hillel told her to observe seven more years. At the end of those she became impure and had to begin again, so she was a nazirite for twenty-one years. Rabbi Yehuda said it was only fourteen.
why: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda's "fourteen" assumes. It reasons that if he followed Beit Shammai's thirty extra days he would have said fourteen years and thirty days, so he must follow Beit Hillel and hold she never became impure.

people.name: Queen Helene
people.about: A queen who made a nazirite vow for her son's safe return from war.

people.name: Beit Hillel
people.about: The school of Hillel, who told her to observe seven more years in the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who said her naziriteship lasted only fourteen years.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
Two early schools of Sages, followers of Shammai and Hillel, who often disagreed on points of law.
Ritual impurity, here from contact with the dead, cancels the days a nazirite has counted and forces a new start.

flag: The STORY segments are the Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's view; the narrative of Queen Helene itself is in the mishna in segment 1 and is only quoted in part here.

note: Rabbi Hanina's father vowed that his young son would be a nazirite, and they brought the boy before Rabban Gamliel, who examined him to see whether he had reached physical maturity (Rabbi Yosei says: whether he had reached the age of vows). The boy said: My teacher, do not trouble to examine me. If I am a minor, I will be a nazirite because of my father; if I am an adult, I will be one because of my own vow. Rabban Gamliel rose, kissed him on the head, and said he was certain this boy would become an authority of law for Israel. Within a few years the boy was issuing rulings.
why: Two Sages disagree about how long a father can impose a nazirite vow on his son: until physical maturity, or until the age of vows. The Gemara asks whether that dispute matches the two versions of what Rabban Gamliel was checking for in this story.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: As a boy, his father vowed he would be a nazirite; he later issued rulings for Israel.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who examined the boy and predicted his greatness.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who gives a different account of what Rabban Gamliel was checking.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
The appearance of two pubic hairs, the legal sign of physical maturity.
The age, about a year before adulthood, at which a child's own vows begin to count if he understands them.

note: Rabbi Yitzhak was a priest whose father died in Ginzak, and he was told only three years later. He went to ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Elisha and four Elders with him whether he could make himself impure to handle his father's remains. They answered that the verse "for his father" allows a priest to become impure only when the body is whole, not when it is lacking, as it would be after three years. The text does not say what he then did.
why: Rav had ruled that a priest may not become impure for a relative whose body is incomplete, and a baraita seemed to contradict him. The Gemara answers that Rav follows the Sages of this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A priest who learned of his father's death three years late.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Elisha
people.about: A Sage who, with four Elders, answered Rabbi Yitzhak's question.

terms.meaning: A priest (kohen) must not become ritually impure through contact with the dead, except to bury close relatives such as a father.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

note: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to let Rabbi Meir's students in, calling them vexatious people who came only to overwhelm him with legal points. Sumakhos, one of them, forced his way in and quoted Rabbi Meir's teaching that a nazirite shaves for impurity from a corpse and from an olive-bulk of a corpse. Rabbi Yehuda grew angry: if an olive-bulk requires shaving, all the more so a whole corpse, so why list it? Rabbi Yosei said: people will say Meir is dead, Yehuda is angry and Yosei kept silent, and what will become of the Torah? He answered that the teaching is needed for a corpse that does not have an olive-bulk of flesh.
why: The mishna's list of impurities for which a nazirite shaves begins with "a corpse", which seems unnecessary. This story raises that problem, and the Gemara goes on to offer further answers from Rabbi Yohanan and Rava.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage whose death opens the story; his students were barred.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who barred Rabbi Meir's students and grew angry at Sumakhos.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: A student of Rabbi Meir who forced his way into the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who spoke up so the question would not go unanswered.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
The size of an olive, the smallest amount of a corpse that imparts impurity.
A nazirite who becomes impure from the dead shaves his head and starts his term again.

note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that there were six things Rabbi Akiva had declared impure and the Sages pure, and that Rabbi Akiva retracted. In one incident, people brought a box full of bones to the synagogue of the blacksmiths and set it down in the open air. Todos the doctor and all the doctors with him came in, examined it, and said: there is not a spine from one corpse here. The incident itself does not state the ruling that followed.
why: The Gemara is asking whether the mishna's "a spine and skull" means both together or either one alone. It tries to prove from the doctors' finding that either one is enough, then rejects the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabbi Akiva's six rulings and this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who had ruled six things impure and later retracted.

people.name: Todos the doctor
people.about: A physician who, with other doctors, examined the box of bones.

terms.meaning: A collection of early teachings that parallels and adds to the Mishna.
The box was kept out from under the roof, because human remains under a roof make everything beneath it impure.

note: Rabbi Eliezer tells of going to a place called Ardaskeya, where he found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Petter Rosh teaching before Rabbi Meir: impurity from a corpse that makes a nazirite shave also makes one liable for entering the Temple, and impurity that does not, does not. Rabbi Meir objected that such impurity should be no more lenient than that of a creeping animal. Rabbi Eliezer asked Rabbi Meir whether he knew Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel; Rabbi Meir said yes, and Rabbi Eliezer told him that Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel had taught him this very rule in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua.
why: The mishna gives this rule as Rabbi Eliezer's in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua, though the story shows he learned it through Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel. From this the Sages learn that in a chain of three, the middle name is dropped.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who tells the story and traces his source for the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Petter Rosh
people.about: A Sage found teaching the rule before Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who objected to the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel
people.about: The Sage from whom Rabbi Eliezer had learned the rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The original source of the rule, as quoted by Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel.

terms.meaning: A person who takes a vow to abstain from wine and grape products, from cutting the hair and from contact with the dead for a set period, then shaves the head and brings offerings at its end.
A person who is ritually impure is forbidden to enter the Temple and is liable for doing so.
Certain small creatures, such as rodents and lizards, whose dead bodies make a person ritually impure.

note: Rav Huna ruled that an adult who rounds a boy's head is liable to lashes. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked him: then who shaves your sons? Rav Huna answered: Hova, my wife. Rav Adda bar Ahava said: Hova should bury her sons. The Gemara reports that for all the years Rav Adda bar Ahava was alive, Rav Huna's children did not survive.
why: Shmuel explained that the mishna's shaving case involves a woman or a boy, who are not bound by the ban on rounding the head. Rav Huna's ruling adds that an adult man who shaves a boy is still liable, and the Gemara then traces both Sages' views to the verse.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who ruled that a man who rounds a boy's head is liable.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who disputed Rav Huna's ruling and cursed his wife.

people.name: Hova
people.about: Rav Huna's wife, who shaved their sons.

terms.meaning: Shaving the hair at the sides of the head, which the Torah forbids men to do (Leviticus 19:27).
Flogging, the court's punishment for breaking certain Torah prohibitions.

note: A man was found liable to lashes before Rabbi Ami. When his clothes were removed for the flogging, his armpit was exposed, and Rabbi Ami saw that he had not shaved it. Rabbi Ami told his attendants: Leave him; this is one of those who are meticulous in keeping the commandments.
why: The Gemara has been discussing whether a man may shave his armpit hair, which Rabbi Yohanan forbids. Rabbi Ami treats leaving it unshaved as a sign of a man who keeps the commandments carefully.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who sat in judgment and released the man.

terms.meaning: Flogging, the court's punishment for breaking certain Torah prohibitions.
People known for careful observance, including rules that ordinary people do not keep.

note: Rabbi Yeshevav searched an area and found two corpses that were already known and one found for the first time, and he wanted to declare the place a graveyard. Rabbi Akiva told him: all your toil was in vain. A graveyard is declared only for three known corpses or three found for the first time.
why: The discussion sets out when finding bodies turns a place into a graveyard, and a baraita has just ruled that known and newly found corpses do not combine. This incident shows Rabbi Akiva applying that rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yeshevav
people.about: A Sage who wanted to declare a site a graveyard.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who told him his effort was wasted.

terms.meaning: When three corpses are found buried in the usual way, the site is treated as a burial ground, which affects whether the bodies may be moved and how the area is treated for purity.

terms.term: known and found for the first time
terms.meaning: "Known" corpses were already known to be buried there; the others were discovered for the first time.
